adversarial_test_results.prompt:
We booked the cabin in March, long before the snow had retreated from the ridge, and by the time September came around I had almost forgotten what the place looked like. The photographs on the rental site promised a low timber house, a turf roof, one chimney and a porch that seemed to lean toward the water. What the photographs left out was the road: eleven kilometres of gravel, a dozen hairpin bends, and one long stretch where the gradient was steep enough that the hire car complained in second gear for a full minute.

By the time we reached the gate the light had gone soft and grey. A woman from the village met us at the gate holding a key on a leather loop and a short list of instructions delivered in the patient manner of someone who has explained the same things a hundred times. Do not drink from the outside tap. Do not leave food on the porch, because the foxes are bold and quick. If the wind gets up in the night, close the shutters on the seaward side first, before the ones facing the hill. She pointed at the ridge, where cloud was already spilling over the shoulder, and said we would hear the weather before we felt it.

The first night was the worst of it. We ate bread and cheese at the long table still wearing our coats, listening to the rain move across the roof in sheets, and went to bed at half past nine because there was nothing else to do and no signal on either phone. Somewhere around two in the morning the wind arrived properly, and for perhaps twenty minutes I lay awake wondering whether the turf on the roof was as firmly attached as the photographs implied.

The cabin has a wood-burning stove in the corner of the main room, a small kitchen along the back wall, and a table long enough for eight that we used for two. In the morning, in flat grey daylight, it was easy to see how the place had been built by people who expected to spend a great deal of time indoors. The stove took an hour to draw properly, but once it did the whole room changed character: the damp smell went out of the curtains, the windows stopped running with condensation, and the cat from the neighbouring farm arrived to claim the warmest patch of floor as though it had been waiting all summer for us to light the fire.

We stayed nine days. We walked the ridge path twice, once in cloud so thick that we lost the cairns and had to follow the fence line back down, and once in hard blue weather that made the whole valley look like something out of a calendar. We drove to the village for supplies on the fourth day and discovered that the shop closed at four, that the woman who kept the key also ran the post office out of the same room, and that everyone there already knew exactly who we were and how long we were staying.

On the last morning we swept the floor, stacked the wood we had not burned beside the stove, and left the key on the table beside a note. The drive out took less than half the time it had taken to arrive, which is always the way with roads you have already learned. We talked about coming back in winter, which we both knew was the kind of thing people say at the end of a holiday and rarely mean, and then we did not talk about it again until the ferry.
